Finite Non-Commutative Centrally Essential Rings of Minimal Order

Adel Abyzov11 1 Kazan (Volga Region) Federal University, Kazan, Russia; email: adel.abyzov@kpfu.ru, Oleg Lyubimtsev22 2 Nizhny Novgorod State University, Department of Algebra, Geometry and Discrete Mathematics, scientific and educational mathematical center ”Mathematics of technologies of the future”, Nizhny Novgorod, Russia; email: oleg_lyubimcev@mail.ru, https://orcid.org/0000-0002-8773-1943., Askar Tuganbaev33 3 National Research University MPEI, Department of Higher Mathematics, Moscow, Russia; Lomonosov Moscow State University, Department of Higher Algebra, Moscow, Russia; tuganbaev@gmail.com, https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9582-3314.

Abstract. A ring RR with non-zero identity element is said to be centrally essential if for any non-zero element aa of RR, there exist non-zero central elements xx and yy such that a​x=yax=y. In the paper, we prove that the minimal order of a finite non-commutative centrally essential ring is equal to 6464. A partial classification of such rings is presented, and the existence of non-isomorphic non-commutative centrally essential rings of minimal order is proved.

Keywords: centrally essential ring, finite local ring.

The work of Adel Abyzov is supported by the Russian Science Foundation (grant 23-21-10086) and performed under the development program of Volga Region Mathematical Center (agreement 075-02-2025-1725/1). The work of Oleg Lyubimtsev is supported by Ministry of Education and Science of the Russian Federation, project H-044-0_2026-2028. The study of Askar Tuganbaev is supported by Russian Science Foundation, project 26-11-00001.

MSC2020 subject classification 16D25, 16R99

1 Introduction

We consider only associative rings with a non-zero identity element and unitary modules. A ring RR is said to be centrally essential if for any non-zero element a∈Ra\in R, there exist non-zero central elements x,y∈Rx,y\in R such that a​x=yax=y.44 4 It is clear that the ring RR with center ZZ is centrally essential if and only if the module RZR_{Z} is an essential extension of the module ZZZ_{Z}. The class of centrally essential rings is a proper extension of the class of commutative rings. In [5, Proposition 3.3], it is proved that semiprime centrally essential rings are commutative. In [4, Example 5.2] a non-commutative centrally essential ring of order 128128 is constructed. In this regard, a natural question arises concerning the minimum possible order of a non-commutative centrally essential ring. We denote by Z⁡(R)Z(R) and J⁡(R)J(R) the center and the Jacobson radical of the ring RR, respectively. It is well known that the Jacobson radical of a right Artinian ring is nilpotent. The smallest nn such that J​(R)n=0J(R)^{n}=0, is called the nilpotence index of J⁡(R)J(R). We write Ann⁡(S)={r∈R|r​S=0}\mathrm{Ann}(S)=\{r\in R\,|\,rS=0\} for the left annihilator of the set SS in the ring RR. A ring RR is said to be local if R/J⁡(R)R/J(R) is a division ring.

The main results of the paper are Theorems 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3.

1.1. Theorem. The smallest finite non-commutative centrally essential ring has 6464 elements.

1.2. Theorem. Let RR be a finite non-commutative centrally essential ring of order 6464. Then:

  1. 1.

    The ring RR is local.

  2. 2.

    The factor ring R/J⁡(R)R/J(R) is isomorphic to the field 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} and the radical J⁡(R)J(R) has order 3232.

  3. 3.

    The center Z⁡(R)Z(R) has order 1616 and the intersection Z0=Z⁡(R)∩J⁡(R)Z_{0}=Z(R)\cap J(R) has order 88.

1.3. Theorem. Within the class of non-commutative centrally essential algebras of order 6464 over the field 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} satisfying the condition J​(R)2⊆Ann⁡(J⁡(R))∩Z⁡(R)J(R)^{2}\subseteq\mathrm{Ann}(J(R))\cap Z(R), there exist exactly two families distinguished by an algebraic invariant – the dimension of the annihilator dim𝔽2W0∈{2,1}\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}W_{0}\in\{2,1\}, where W0=Ann⁡(J⁡(R))∩Z⁡(R)W_{0}=\mathrm{Ann}(J(R))\cap Z(R). These families are described as follows.

Family 1 (dim𝔽2W0=2\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}W_{0}=2)

The algebra has a basis {1,a,b,c,s1,s2}\{1,a,b,c,s_{1},s_{2}\}, with J⁡(R)=⟨a,b,c,s1,s2⟩𝔽2J(R)=\langle a,b,c,s_{1},s_{2}\rangle_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}, Z⁡(R)=⟨1,c,s1,s2⟩𝔽2Z(R)=\langle 1,c,s_{1},s_{2}\rangle_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}, and W0=⟨s1,s2⟩𝔽2W_{0}=\langle s_{1},s_{2}\rangle_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}. The multiplication of the basis elements of the radical is defined by the rules: a​c=c​a=s1ac=ca=s_{1}; b​c=c​b=s2bc=cb=s_{2}; a​b=s1ab=s_{1}, b​a=0ba=0; c2=0c^{2}=0. The elements s1s_{1} and s2s_{2} annihilate J⁡(R)J(R). The squares a2=αa^{2}=\alpha and b2=βb^{2}=\beta are parametrized by elements α,β∈W0\alpha,\beta\in W_{0}.

Family 2 (dim𝔽2W0=1\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}W_{0}=1)

The algebra has a basis {1,a,b,c1,c2,w}\{1,a,b,c_{1},c_{2},w\}, J⁡(R)=⟨a,b,c1,c2,w⟩𝔽2J(R)=\langle a,b,c_{1},c_{2},w\rangle_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}, Z⁡(R)=⟨1,c1,c2,w⟩𝔽2Z(R)=\langle 1,c_{1},c_{2},w\rangle_{\mathbb{F}_{2}} and W0=⟨w⟩𝔽2W_{0}=\langle w\rangle_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}. The multiplication of basis elements of the radical is defined by the rules: a​c1=c1​a=wac_{1}=c_{1}a=w, b​c1=c1​b=0bc_{1}=c_{1}b=0; a​c2=c2​a=0ac_{2}=c_{2}a=0, b​c2=c2​b=wbc_{2}=c_{2}b=w; a​b=wab=w, b​a=0ba=0; c12=c22=c1​c2=c2​c1=0c_{1}^{2}=c_{2}^{2}=c_{1}c_{2}=c_{2}c_{1}=0. The element ww annihilates the radical J⁡(R)J(R). The squares a2=α​wa^{2}=\alpha w and b2=β​wb^{2}=\beta w are parametrized by scalars α,β∈𝔽2\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{F}_{2}.

2 Proof of Theorem 1.1

Theorem 1.1 follows from Lemmas 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3.

2.1. Lemma. There do not exist finite non-commutative centrally essential rings of order ≤32\leq 32.

Proof. Let RR be a finite non-commutative centrally essential ring of minimal order. Then RR is a local ring. Indeed, in any centrally essential ring, all idempotents are central; see [5, Lemma 2.3]. Lifting idempotents modulo a nilpotent ideal allows a unique decomposition of a finite ring RR into a direct product of finite local rings. It is clear that a direct product of such rings is centrally essential if and only if each of its factors is a centrally essential ring. If there were more than one factor, then a non-commutative factor would have strictly smaller order, which contradicts the minimality of RR.

Let |R|=pn|R|=p^{n}, Z=Z⁡(R)Z=Z(R), J=J⁡(R)J=J(R) and the factor ring R/J≅𝔽qR/J\cong\mathbb{F}_{q}, where q=pfq=p^{f}. We set Z0=Z∩JZ_{0}=Z\cap J. Let us obtain an upper bound for the cardinality of the set Z0Z_{0}. Since the ring RR is not commutative, the index of its center as an additive subgroup, [R:Z][R:Z], is at least p2p^{2}. Indeed if [R:Z]=p[R:Z]=p, then the additive factor group R/ZR/Z is a cyclic group generated by some residue class a+Za+Z. Then any element of the ring is of the form z+k​az+ka, where z∈Zz\in Z, k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z} and [z1+k1​a,z2+k2​a]=0[z_{1}+k_{1}a,z_{2}+k_{2}a]=0, i.e. the ring RR is commutative. Consequently, |Z|≤|R|/p2=pn−2|Z|\leq|R|/p^{2}=p^{n-2}. Since 1∈Z1\in Z and 1∉J1\notin J, we have that Z0=Z∩JZ_{0}=Z\cap J is a proper subgroup in ZZ. Since ZZ is a finite pp-group, the index of any of its proper subgroup is not less than pp. Therefore, |Z|≥p​|Z0||Z|\geq p|Z_{0}|. Combining the inequalities, we obtain an upper bound for any prime integer pp:

|Z0|≤|Z|p≤pn−2p=pn−3.|Z_{0}|\leq\frac{|Z|}{p}\leq\frac{p^{n-2}}{p}=p^{n-3}.

Now we obtain a lower bound on the cardinality of the set Z0Z_{0}. First, note that if J=0J=0, then the ring RR is semiprime. However, semiprime centrally essential rings are commutative; see [5, Proposition 3.3]. Consequently, JJ is a nilpotent ideal with index of nilpotency kk, where k≥2k\geq 2. Since JJ is a nilpotent ideal with nilpotence index kk, it follows from [1, Lemma 2.4] that Jk−1∩Z⁡(R)J^{k-1}\cap Z(R) is a central ideal. In addition, since the ring RR is centrally essential, we have Jk−1∩Z⁡(R)≠0J^{k-1}\cap Z(R)\neq 0. Therefore, the annihilator Ann⁡(J)\mathrm{Ann}(J) contains non-zero central element z1∈W0=Ann⁡(J)∩Z0z_{1}\in W_{0}=\mathrm{Ann}(J)\cap Z_{0}. Since the ring RR is not commutative, it follows from [3] that there exists an element r∈J∖Z0r\in J\setminus Z_{0}. Then there exists an element x∈Z∖{0}x\in Z\setminus\{0\} such that r​x∈Z∖{0}rx\in Z\setminus\{0\}. If x∉Jx\notin J, then xx is invertible in RR, whence r∈Z​x−1=Zr\in Zx^{-1}=Z and r∈Z0r\in Z_{0}. This is a contradiction. Therefore, x∈Z0∖{0}x\in Z_{0}\setminus\{0\}. Since r​z1=0rz_{1}=0 and r​x≠0rx\neq 0, we have that x≠z1x\neq z_{1}. Consequently, Z0Z_{0} contains at least three distinct elements 00, z1z_{1} and xx. We obtain that |Z0|≥3|Z_{0}|\geq 3. We also remark that for p=2p=2, we have that |Z0|≥4|Z_{0}|\geq 4, since the order is a power of two. Consequently, 3≤|Z0|≤pn−33\leq|Z_{0}|\leq p^{n-3}. We verify possible orders |R|≤32|R|\leq 32. If p≥3p\geq 3, it follows from |R|≤32|R|\leq 32 that n≤3n\leq 3. Then |Z0|≤p3−3=1|Z_{0}|\leq p^{3-3}=1; this contradicts the fact that |Z0|≥3|Z_{0}|\geq 3. Therefore, the characteristic of the residue field cannot be odd.

Let p=2p=2. We have |Z0|≤2n−3|Z_{0}|\leq 2^{n-3}. Since |Z0|≥4|Z_{0}|\geq 4, we have that n≥5n\geq 5. By considering |R|≤32|R|\leq 32, we obtain n=5n=5, that is |R|=32|R|=32. In addition, |Z0|≤25−3=4|Z_{0}|\leq 2^{5-3}=4, whence |Z0|=4|Z_{0}|=4. We consider possible variants for the degree ff (where q=2fq=2^{f}). In a finite local ring of order pnp^{n} with residue field 𝔽pf\mathbb{F}_{p^{f}}, the degree ff must be a divisor of nn. We consider a homomorphism of additive groups Lx:J→Z0L_{x}\colon J\to Z_{0} such that r↦r​xr\mapsto rx. It follows from the above and the inclusion Z02⊆Z0Z^{2}_{0}\subseteq Z_{0} that LxL_{x} is well-defined and ker⁡(Lx)⊆Z0\ker(L_{x})\subseteq Z_{0}. Since |Im​(Lx)|≤|Z0|=4|\text{Im}(L_{x})|\leq|Z_{0}|=4, we have |J|/|ker⁡(Lx)|≤4|J|/|\ker(L_{x})|\leq 4, whence |ker⁡(Lx)|≥16/4=4|\ker(L_{x})|\geq 16/4=4. Thus, ker⁡(Lx)=Z0\ker(L_{x})=Z_{0}, and LxL_{x} induces a bijection J/Z0→Z0J/Z_{0}\to Z_{0}. There exists u∈Ju\in J such that u​x=xux=x, implying (1−u)​x=0(1-u)x=0. Since u∈Ju\in J, the element (1−u)(1-u) is invertible. Hence, x=0x=0. This is a contradiction. Thus, all possible cases for |R|≤32|R|\leq 32 are ruled out, and the lemma is proved. □\square

2.2. Lemma. There are no finite non-commutative centrally essential rings with orders strictly greater than 32 and strictly less than 64.

Proof. Let RR be a finite non-commutative centrally essential ring, 32<|R|<6432<|R|<64. A ring RR is decomposed into a direct product of finite local centrally essential rings:

R=R1×R2×⋯×Rk.R=R_{1}\times R_{2}\times\dots\times R_{k}.

Let R1R_{1} be a non-commutative factor. If k≥2k\geq 2, then the order of the factor |R1||R_{1}| is a proper divisor of order |R||R|. The greatest proper divisor of any positive integer ≤63\leq 63 does not exceed [63/2]=31[63/2]=31. Therefore, |R1|≤31|R_{1}|\leq 31. By Lemma 2.1, such a ring does not exist. If k=1k=1, then the ring RR is local and its order must be a power of prime integer. Among the powers of prime numbers in the interval (32,64)(32,64), there are only prime numbers and the square of a prime number, 49=7249=7^{2}. Every ring of prime order or of order p2p^{2} is always commutative; see [2]. This is a contradiction. □\square

2.3. Lemma. There exists a non-commutative centrally essential ring consisting of 6464 elements.

Proof. We construct a 66-dimensional algebra RR over the field of two elements 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}. The order of such an algebra is equal to |R|=26=64|R|=2^{6}=64. We define the following basis of the algebra: {1,a,b,c,s1,s2}\{1,a,b,c,s_{1},s_{2}\}. The unity 11 is a multiplicative identity element. The Jacobson radical JJ is equal to ⟨a,b,c,s1,s2⟩𝔽2\langle a,b,c,s_{1},s_{2}\rangle_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}. For basis elements of the radical, we set

a2=b2=c2=0,a​b=s1,b​a=0,a​c=c​a=s1,b​c=c​b=s2,a^{2}=b^{2}=c^{2}=0,ab=s_{1},ba=0,ac=ca=s_{1},bc=cb=s_{2},
s1​x=x​s1=0,s2​x=x​s2=0for all​x∈J.s_{1}x=xs_{1}=0,s_{2}x=xs_{2}=0\quad\mbox{for all}\,x\in J.

Since the product of any two elements from JJ belongs to the subspace S=⟨s1,s2⟩𝔽2S=\langle s_{1},s_{2}\rangle_{\mathbb{F}_{2}} and S⊆Ann⁡(J)S\subseteq\mathrm{Ann}(J), we have that J3=0J^{3}=0 and the identity (x​y)​z=x⁡(y​z)(xy)z=x(yz) is trivially true. Next, since a​b=s1≠0ab=s_{1}\neq 0 and b​a=0ba=0, we have that the ring RR is not commutative.

Let us find the center Z⁡(R)Z(R) of the ring RR. Let x∈Rx\in R, then x=k0​1+ka​a+kb​b+kc​c+k1​s1+k2​s2x=k_{0}1+k_{a}a+k_{b}b+k_{c}c+k_{1}s_{1}+k_{2}s_{2}, where ki∈𝔽2k_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}. We have:

[x,a]=x​a−a​x=kb​[b,a]+kc​[c,a]=kb​(0−s1)+kc​(s1−s1)=kb​s1,[x,a]=xa-ax=k_{b}[b,a]+k_{c}[c,a]=k_{b}(0-s_{1})+k_{c}(s_{1}-s_{1})=k_{b}s_{1},

whence kb=0k_{b}=0. Next,

[x,b]=x​b−b​x=ka​[a,b]+kc​[c,b]=ka​s1+kc​(s2−s2)=ka​s1,[x,b]=xb-bx=k_{a}[a,b]+k_{c}[c,b]=k_{a}s_{1}+k_{c}(s_{2}-s_{2})=k_{a}s_{1},

whence ka=0k_{a}=0. Since [x,c]=0[x,c]=0, we have that Z⁡(R)=⟨1,c,s1,s2⟩𝔽2Z(R)=\langle 1,c,s_{1},s_{2}\rangle_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}.

Every non-central element r∈R∖Z⁡(R)r\in R\setminus Z(R) is of the form r=ka​a+kb​b+zr=k_{a}a+k_{b}b+z, where z∈Z⁡(R)z\in Z(R) and (ka,kb)≠(0,0)(k_{a},k_{b})\neq(0,0). Then

r​c=(ka​a+kb​b+k0​1+kc​c+k1​s1+k2​s2)​c=k0​c+ka​s1+kb​s2.rc=(k_{a}a+k_{b}b+k_{0}1+k_{c}c+k_{1}s_{1}+k_{2}s_{2})c=k_{0}c+k_{a}s_{1}+k_{b}s_{2}.

Since the basis vectors c,s1,s2c,s_{1},s_{2} are linearly independent and at least one of the coefficients ka,kbk_{a},k_{b} is non-zero, it follows that r​c≠0rc\neq 0 and r​c∈Z⁡(R)rc\in Z(R). Therefore, the algebra RR is centrally essential. □\square

3 Proof of Theorem 1.2

1. Since all idempotents in a centrally essential ring are central, a finite centrally essential ring decomposes uniquely into a direct product of local centrally essential rings. If the ring RR has a non-trivial decomposition, then the order of the non-commutative factor does not exceed 64/2=3264/2=32. However, by Lemma 2.1, there are no non-commutative centrally essential rings of order ≤32\leq 32. Consequently, the ring RR is local.

2. Let R/J⁡(R)≅𝔽qR/J(R)\cong\mathbb{F}_{q}. Since |R|=64=26|R|=64=2^{6}, we have q=2fq=2^{f}. Thus, ff must be a divisor of 66, i.e., f∈{1,2,3,6}f\in\{1,2,3,6\}. If q=64q=64 (f=6f=6), then |J⁡(R)|=1|J(R)|=1. Consequently, the ring R≅𝔽64R\cong\mathbb{F}_{64} is commutative, which contradicts the theorem’s hypothesis. We prove that q=2q=2 (f=1f=1). We assume that q≥4q\geq 4. It follows from [R:Z(R)]≥4[R:Z(R)]\geq 4 that |Z⁡(R)|≤16|Z(R)|\leq 16. Since [Z(R):Z0]≥2[Z(R):Z_{0}]\geq 2, we have that |Z0|≤8|Z_{0}|\leq 8. The set W0=Ann⁡(J)∩Z0W_{0}=\mathrm{Ann}(J)\cap Z_{0} is non-zero (see the proof of Lemma 2.1), consequently |W0|≥2|W_{0}|\geq 2. Since the ring RR is centrally essential, we have that W0⊊Z0W_{0}\subsetneq Z_{0}, whence |Z0|≥4|Z_{0}|\geq 4.

Let q=8q=8 (f=3f=3). Then |J⁡(R)|=8|J(R)|=8. From the estimate obtained earlier we have 4≤|Z0|≤84\leq|Z_{0}|\leq 8. If |Z0|=8|Z_{0}|=8, then Z0=J⁡(R)⊆Z⁡(R)Z_{0}=J(R)\subseteq Z(R) and the ring RR is commutative. If |Z0|=4|Z_{0}|=4, then |J⁡(R)/Z0|=2|J(R)/Z_{0}|=2. Therefore, the radical J⁡(R)=⟨Z0,j0⟩J(R)=\langle Z_{0},j_{0}\rangle is commutative. The canonical epimorphism of the groups of units R∗→(R/J⁡(R))∗≅𝔽8∗R^{*}\to(R/J(R))^{*}\cong\mathbb{F}_{8}^{*} has a kernel 1+J⁡(R)1+J(R) of order 88. Consequently, there exists an element ω∈R∗\omega\in R^{*} of multiplicative order 77 such that its coset ω+J⁡(R)\omega+J(R) generates the field R/J⁡(R)R/J(R). The action by conjugation by ω\omega on the two-element quotient group J⁡(R)/Z0J(R)/Z_{0} is trivial; therefore, ω​j0​ω−1=j0+z\omega j_{0}\omega^{-1}=j_{0}+z for some z∈Z0z\in Z_{0}. Multiplying on the right by ω\omega, we obtain ω​j0=j0​ω+z​ω\omega j_{0}=j_{0}\omega+z\omega. Since z∈Z⁡(R)z\in Z(R), applying this relation repeatedly yields ωk​j0=j0​ωk+k​z​ωk\omega^{k}j_{0}=j_{0}\omega^{k}+kz\omega^{k}. For k=7k=7, we have ω7=1\omega^{7}=1, which implies j0=j0+7​zj_{0}=j_{0}+7z. Because Z0Z_{0} is a finite 22-group, multiplication by the odd number 77 is an automorphism of the group Z0Z_{0}. It follows that z=0z=0, and thus ω\omega commutes with j0j_{0}. Since ω\omega and J⁡(R)J(R) generate the entire ring RR, and J⁡(R)J(R) is commutative, the ring RR is commutative. This is a contradiction.

Suppose q=4q=4 (f=2f=2). Then |J⁡(R)|=16|J(R)|=16. Let us consider the possible orders |Z0|∈{4,8}|Z_{0}|\in\{4,8\}. Suppose |Z0|=4|Z_{0}|=4. Then |W0|=2|W_{0}|=2. Choose an element c∈Z0∖W0c\in Z_{0}\setminus W_{0}. Following the same steps as in the proof of Lemma 2.1, one can verify that the homomorphism Lc:J⁡(R)→Z0L_{c}:J(R)\to Z_{0} (defined by r↦r​cr\mapsto rc) induces a bijection J⁡(R)/Z0→Z0J(R)/Z_{0}\to Z_{0}, which leads to a contradiction. Finally, assume |Z0|=8|Z_{0}|=8. Then |J⁡(R)/Z0|=16/8=2|J(R)/Z_{0}|=16/8=2, which implies that J⁡(R)=⟨Z0,j0⟩J(R)=\langle Z_{0},j_{0}\rangle is a commutative ideal. Analogous to the case q=8q=8, choose an element ω∈R∗\omega\in R^{*} of multiplicative order 33 such that its image generates R/J⁡(R)≅𝔽4R/J(R)\cong\mathbb{F}_{4}. This element acts trivially on J⁡(R)/Z0J(R)/Z_{0}: ω​j0​ω−1=j0+z\omega j_{0}\omega^{-1}=j_{0}+z for some z∈Z0z\in Z_{0}. Raising this to the third power yields j0=j0+3​zj_{0}=j_{0}+3z, which implies z=0z=0 and ω​j0=j0​ω\omega j_{0}=j_{0}\omega. Since ω\omega and J⁡(R)J(R) generate RR, the ring RR is commutative. This is a contradiction.

Thus, the assumption q≥4q\geq 4 leads to a contradiction in all cases. Consequently, R/J⁡(R)≅𝔽2R/J(R)\cong\mathbb{F}_{2} and |J⁡(R)|=64/2=32|J(R)|=64/2=32.

3. Since the ring RR is not commutative, the index of its center as an additive group, [R:Z(R)][R:Z(R)], is at least 4. Therefore, |Z⁡(R)|≤64/4=16|Z(R)|\leq 64/4=16.
